Two-Arm Experiment with a Covariate

Source: vignettes/two_arm_covariate.Rmd
two_arm_covariate.Rmd

We are often told to “control” for various different variables that might be related to our independent or dependent variables. Does it always make sense to control? Or are there instances when we better estimate the effect of our explanatory variable on our dependent variable by ignoring potential control variables?

We declare a design in which a researcher seeks to understand the causal effect of explanatory variable, ZZ, on outcome variable YY. A covariate, WW, might be correlated with either or neither of these variables.

In this particular setup, you do better by controlling – even in an experiment – except when the covariate is correlated with the explanatory variable but not with the outcome.

Design Declaration

  • Model:

    Our model of the world specifies a population of NN units that have three observable variables. The binary treatment variable, ZZ, is potentially correlated with the covariate, WW. The outcome variable, YY, is a function of the treatment variable, and may also be correlated with WW. We refer to the correlations between WW and ZZ and between WW and YY as ρWZ\rho_{WZ} and ρWY\rho_{WY}, respectively.

  • Inquiry:

    We want to know the average of all units’ differences in treated and untreated potential outcomes – the average treatment effect on the outcome of interest: E[Yi(Z=1)−Yi(Z=0)]E[Y_i(Z = 1) - Y_i(Z = 0)].

  • Data strategy:

    The variable ZZ is not assigned to units by researchers – rather, it is assigned by the unobservable process, UZU_Z, which may be correlated with UWU_W.

  • Answer strategy:

    We consider three answer strategies. The first does not control for WW when estimating the effect of ZZ on YY. The second controls for the average effect of WW on YY when estimating the effect of ZZ on YY. The third uses an estimator that averages over differences in the effect of ZZ on YY for different levels of WW.

N <- 100
a_R <- 0
b_R <- 1
a_Y <- 0
b_Y <- 1
rho <- 0

population <- declare_population(N = N, u_R = rnorm(N), u_Y = rnorm(N, 
    mean = rho * u_R, sd = sqrt(1 - rho^2)))
potential_outcomes_R <- declare_potential_outcomes(R ~ (a_R + 
    b_R * Z > u_R))
potential_outcomes_Y <- declare_potential_outcomes(Y ~ (a_Y + 
    b_Y * Z > u_Y))
estimand_1 <- declare_inquiry(mean(R_Z_1 - R_Z_0), label = "ATE on R")
estimand_2 <- declare_inquiry(mean(Y_Z_1 - Y_Z_0), label = "ATE on Y")
estimand_3 <- declare_inquiry(mean((Y_Z_1 - Y_Z_0)[R == 1]), 
    label = "ATE on Y (Given R)")
assignment <- declare_assignment(Z = complete_ra(N, prob = 0.5))
reveal <- declare_reveal(outcome_variables = c("R", "Y"))
observed <- declare_step(Y_obs = ifelse(R, Y, NA), handler = fabricate)
estimator_1 <- declare_estimator(R ~ Z, term = "Z", inquiry = estimand_1, 
    label = "DIM on R")
estimator_2 <- declare_estimator(Y_obs ~ Z, term = "Z", inquiry = c(estimand_2, 
    estimand_3), label = "DIM on Y_obs")
estimator_3 <- declare_estimator(Y ~ Z, term = "Z", inquiry = c(estimand_2, 
    estimand_3), label = "DIM on Y")
two_arm_attrition_design <- population + potential_outcomes_R + 
    potential_outcomes_Y + assignment + reveal + observed + 
    estimand_1 + estimand_2 + estimand_3 + estimator_1 + 
    estimator_2 + estimator_3

Takeaways 

designs <- expand_design(
  designer = two_arm_covariate_designer,
  N = 30, rho_WY = c(0,.8), rho_WZ = c(0,.8), h = .5)
diagnoses <- diagnose_designs(designs, sims = 25)

No controls 0.0 0.8 -0.07 0.37

No controls 0.8 0.8 -1.27 1.34
With controls 0.8 0.8 0.02 0.29
Lin 0.8 0.8 0.01 0.27

  • When WW is independent of both ZZ and YY, it really doesn’t make much of a difference if you control or not

  • When WW is predictive of YY but not correlated with ZZ, you do strictly better by controlling for WW. This is the case, for example, of experiments with prognostic covariates.

  • When WW is correlated with ZZ but not with YY, we can actually minimize root mean square error by not controlling. We’re better off leaving WW out because, while controlling provides no information on YY, it introduces colinearity between WW and ZZ.

  • In the final three rows, we have a case of confounding: WW is correlated with both sides of the regression equation. Here the bias when we don’t control is very high; controlling helps a lot.
